cards.title: Deconstruct Any Ad Into Messaging and Creative DNA
cards.summary: Break every paid social ad into seven messaging components plus the CAST video elements so you can diagnose why it works and clone it systematically.
cards.use_when: Auditing a competitor's winning ad or your own top performer to decide what to iterate on next for your store's creative pipeline.
steps: Treat every ad as two layers: messaging (what you say) and creative (what it looks like — video or image).
Split messaging into three questions: WHO = the segment; WHAT = concept, angle, mechanism, copy blocks; HOW = hook and format.

For video, add the CAST breakdown: Conceit (media format the ad pretends to be, e.g. interview), Actor, Style (visual gloss — realistic, Pixar, claymation), Terrain (environment), Setup (captions, B-roll, inserts, split screen, hook stacking).

Worked example from the source: an anti-aging ad had segment = broad anti-aging; concept = men cheat because their wife stops glowing; angle = confessional whistleblower; mechanism = low-molecular-weight collagen and hyaluronic acid absorbing into skin; format = confessional/interview-style; conceit = pretends to be an interview; actor = high-end escort; style = realistic; terrain = dark studio; setup = captions plus testimonial/demo splices.
When an ad wins, ask which element is responsible — the concept alone, the actor alone, or the combination — and rotate the others.
Apply this to your store by writing the DNA breakdown for your top 5 and bottom 5 ads, then hypothesizing what to keep and what to swap.
caveats: The grammar describes most of an ad but not all of it; other components exist.
This is an analytical framework, not proof any single element causes performance.

cards.title: Build Audience Segments From Outcome × Demographic × Facet
cards.summary: Define granular ad segments by multiplying desired outcomes, demographic traits and specific facets, then write ads aimed at each slice for horizontal scaling.
cards.use_when: Expanding creative targeting for a supplements, health, skincare or similar store by finding untapped customer slices to write dedicated ads for.
steps: Treat a segment as a slice of a market defined on three dimensions: outcome (core thing they want or don't want), demographic (gender, race, age, buyer type), and facet (a specific condition, state or event).
List outcomes for your product; for a testosterone product the source gives examples like better sex, losing man boobs, losing weight.
List facets such as smoker, on finasteride, considering TRT, vegetarian/vegan, GLP-1 user, diabetic, runner.

Multiply dimensions as few or as many as you want to get segments like 'all men who want better sex', 'all black men struggling with erections', or 'men over 50 on finasteride who want to lose weight'.
Run these as separate ad concepts so the algorithm serves each segment independently.
Call this horizontal scaling, and prioritize new outcomes and sub-outcomes plus multiplying facets as the highest-gain area.
caveats: Segment definitions must respect ad platform targeting and health-claim policies; verify current rules.
Granularity is a spectrum — the source says you can go broad or narrow, not that one is universally better.

cards.title: Separate Concept, Angle and Mechanism Before Writing Copy
cards.summary: Distinguish the core idea (concept), how you present it (angle), and why the product works (mechanism) so hooks and copy are built on clearly defined ideas.
cards.use_when: Planning the messaging layer of a new ad or landing page angle for a product whose core claim is still vague.
steps: Write the concept as one plain sentence — the core idea you're communicating. Source example: too much vitamin D is bad for you.
Choose an angle: the same concept can be shown as a conspiracy about the vitamin D industry, a whistleblower, or a side-by-side comparison of two people with and without vitamin D.
Define the mechanism in two parts — the unique mechanism of the problem (why do I have this problem?) and the unique mechanism of the solution (how is your product perfect for it?).
Prefer mechanisms that are simple, intuitive and new; typically one problem and one solution.
Strengthen the mechanism by tying in founder story, product creation story, unique features/ingredients, unique characterizations and moments in time to deepen positioning.
Only after concept, angle and mechanism are clear, write the hook from that idea so messaging stays coherent.
caveats: The source allows multi-problem/multi-solution mechanisms but flags the one-problem/one-solution form as the typical best pattern.
Mechanism claims must be substantiated to avoid regulatory issues in health and supplement categories.

cards.title: Use the Six Copy Blocks as a Persuasion Checklist
cards.summary: Audit every ad and PDP against pain, promise, proof, curiosity, constraints and conditions — the Lego pieces of persuasive copy.
cards.use_when: Reviewing ad scripts or product page copy before launch to find which persuasion blocks are missing or weak.
steps: List the six copy blocks: pain, promise, proof, curiosity, constraints, conditions.

Score each ad's strength on each block — in the source's dissection, one ad had pain, promise and curiosity present but weak, and other blocks missing; a second ad had all blocks present but proof was weak.
Treat it as a checklist: more blocks present and stronger usually means a better ad.
Where proof is weak, strengthen it with testimonials, demo splices or ingredient data rather than adding new claims.
Use the audit output to decide the single block to fix on the next iteration instead of rewriting the whole ad.
caveats: The source calls this a typical pattern, not a guaranteed causal rule; having all six does not ensure an ad wins.
Constraint and condition blocks are context-specific and may not fit every offer.

cards.title: Write Hooks in Four Steps: Isolate, Commit, Deep Fry, Bang
cards.summary: Turn a basic product idea into a scroll-stopping hook by adding contrast, novelty and stakes, then emotional trigger words and open loops.
cards.use_when: Drafting the first 3 seconds of a video ad or the headline of a static ad for a new product angle.
steps: Isolate the idea: start from the core product mechanism — e.g. a magnesium cream that's better than capsules for pain.
Commit to the idea fully before embellishing it.

Deep fry it: add contrast, surprise, novelty, nuance and stakes. Ask 'why is it better?' — it absorbs through skin — then stretch the feature into something interesting: a specific magnesium with no attached molecule becomes 'naked magnesium'.

Make it bang: add emotional trigger words, keep it simple, prioritize the best information, and add open loops. Example result: a grandma used a weird naked magnesium trick that fixed her back pain in two weeks — contrast between grandma and naked, emotional charge on weird/naked, and an open loop from 'trick'.
Treat hooks as roughly 90% of the messaging job and iterate multiple hooks per single ad idea.
caveats: The source explicitly says the example hook is illustrative, not proven to work — do not treat it as a template that guarantees results.
Emotional and 'naked'-style framing must fit brand and platform policy.

cards.title: Pretend-Format Ads: Pick a Conceit That Fits the Offer
cards.summary: Choose the media format your ad pretends to be — interview, whistleblower, timeline, personification — and apply proven formats to winning concepts.
cards.use_when: Deciding the structural format for a new ad, or refreshing a winning concept that is fatiguing.
steps: Understand format as the structure and way you approach the idea; formats trend and rotate over time.
Recognize the recurring formats the source names: whistleblower, timeline ads, personification (e.g. animated body parts), and Wall Street Journal style (comparing two people's paths side by side).
Note that not every ad needs a conceit — when nothing is being imitated, skip that CAST element (the personified-arteries ad had no conceit).
When you have a winning concept or angle, apply it to a known winning format and winning style to shortcut production.
When iterating a winner, change the format first: keep concept and actor, then test the same ad as a podcast, an on-stage talk, a street interview or a slice-of-life film.
caveats: Formats are trend-dependent — what is winning now may not be next quarter, so monitor current accounts.
Pretending to be a real media format may raise disclosure or authenticity concerns depending on platform policy.

cards.title: Three Creative Types Across Three Funnel Stages
cards.summary: Classify creatives as branded, template or native, and place each at bottom-, middle- or top-of-funnel to keep the pipeline balanced.
cards.use_when: Auditing your ad account's creative mix to see whether every funnel stage has the right creative type for your store.
steps: Sort every creative into one of three types: branded, template (follows a pre-assigned template structure), and native (looks like realistic, non-ad content).
Map creatives against funnel position: bottom, middle and top of funnel.
For top of funnel, favor native and trend-driven styles that blend into the feed; for bottom of funnel, favor clearer branded or direct-response formats.
Use the matrix to spot empty cells — e.g. no native top-of-funnel tests or no branded bottom-of-funnel retargeting — and fill those gaps in the next production cycle.
Re-evaluate the classification regularly as formats evolve.
caveats: The source offers this as a mental model without detailed examples; exact assignments depend on your market and platform.
Funnel-stage definitions vary by advertiser; align with your own account structure rather than an absolute rule.

cards.title: Use the CAST System to Clone Winning Videos Element by Element
cards.summary: Break a winning video into Conceit, Actor, Style, Terrain and Setup, then rotate one element at a time to scale iterations efficiently.
cards.use_when: Producing multiple video ad variants from a single proven winner for a store without losing what made it work.
steps: Decompose the video: Conceit = the media format it pretends to be; Actor = who appears (including personified objects like arteries or product); Style = visual gloss (realistic, Pixar, claymation, felt); Terrain = environment and setting; Setup = chunky production elements like captions, B-roll, inserts, cutaways, split screen, hook stacking.

Verify against the source's example: the personified-arteries ad had no conceit, actors were the arteries/clogs/product/ingredients, style was Pixar-like, terrain was inside the body, setup was captions only.
Hypothesize which element drives the win — the concept, the actor, or the combination.
If the actor drives it (e.g. the escort-confessional ad), make more ads with that actor type and rotate angle, mechanism, hook and format.
If the concept drives it, keep the concept and swap actor, style or terrain.
Produce iterations by selling a winning reference to your editor with the specific element changed, rather than briefing from scratch.
caveats: The framework approximates the ad but does not fully describe it; use judgment on which elements matter.
Role-based scripting or actors may face platform impersonation or disclosure policies.

cards.title: Pattern-Detect Winners and Losers With Shared Grammar
cards.summary: Apply the messaging/CAST vocabulary consistently so you (or AI tools) can tag ads and surface which concepts, formats or styles actually trend.
cards.use_when: Reviewing account and competitor performance data to decide which creative elements to double down on for your store.
steps: Tag every ad you see — your own, competitor, and organic content — using the same element labels (segment, concept, angle, mechanism, copy blocks, hook, format; conceit, actor, style, terrain, setup).
Ask of each ad: why is this working, kind of working, or not working?
Compare across sources: your account, competitor accounts, and the outside world (organic content, forums, comments, reviews).
Form explicit hypotheses from the detected patterns and test them as new ad variations.
Use consistent labels so that AI tools can process the tagged data and detect correlations you'd miss manually.
Feed findings back into rotation decisions — which element to change, which to hold.
caveats: Pattern detection produces hypotheses, not proof; correlation in your own data may not transfer to competitors or other markets.
AI-assisted tagging quality depends on your labeling consistency and model; verify outputs.

cards.title: Find Account Gaps With the Segment-Format Matrix
cards.summary: Identify creative whitespace by crossing possible segments with possible formats and styles, then flag which cells competitors cover and you don't.
cards.use_when: Planning the next month's creative testing calendar for a store and tired of producing variations on the same theme.
steps: Build a matrix of your possible segments against possible formats and styles.
Mark which combinations you've already run and which competitors are running.
Flag gaps: if competitors are heavy on timeline ads and you have none, that's a gap; if they use a new style you don't, that's another gap.
Also mine segments buried in comments and Amazon reviews as untapped targeting opportunities.
Prioritize the gaps for the next test batch, mixing in proven cells so the account keeps working while you test net-new areas.
Repeat the matrix review regularly as formats and competitor behavior shift.
caveats: The source gives no numeric target for how many gap tests to run; it depends on production capacity and spend.
Testing net-new formats typically has a lower hit rate than iterating winners.

cards.title: STORMING: Diversify Idea Sources So You Never Run Out
cards.summary: Generate ad ideas from seven distinct sources — Swipes, Templates, Organic research, Matrix, Internal vectors, New styles, Gambit — to raise your hit rate.
cards.use_when: Filling a creative pipeline for frequent ad testing so ideas are not all rip-offs of the same competitor or your own brain.
steps: Swipes: pull winning ad ideas from competitor accounts.
Templates: reuse proven formats and structures.
Organic research: mine comments, Amazon reviews, Facebook comments, forums and new papers for language and angles.
Matrix: cross segments with formats to reveal missing combinations.
Internal vectors: identify patterns inside your own account data.
New styles: adopt trending visual styles such as Pixar or claymation looks.
Gambit: allow shower-thought wild cards — low hit rate but occasionally bangers when executed well.
Track which source each test came from so you can see whether your diversification is real.
caveats: Gambits are explicitly low-probability; don't let them crowd out higher-likelihood work.
Sourcing organic content as idea input doesn't license copying it directly.

cards.title: Make Strategic Bets: Cheap Iterations Usually Beat Net-New Ads
cards.summary: When choosing what to test with limited production and spend, prioritize rotating new conceits, facets, sub-outcomes or styles onto already-winning ideas.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to produce this week when editor capacity and testing budget are the real constraints for your store.
steps: Recognize the real bottleneck: at 10 ads/week you have few shots; at 50 it matters less; editor capacity and how many ads you can actually test are hard limits even with AI.

Answer explicit strategy questions per batch: iterate a winner or make something net new? Which sources to pull from? Which ideas to prioritize? More proven or more wild card? New segments or deepen existing ones? Focus on new styles, formats or conceits?

Lean toward the source's stated high-leverage defaults: new conceits/formats on winning ideas, new facets and sub-outcomes on winning ideas, new styles on winning ideas, and applying winning styles across past winning ideas.
Keep it simple — the source says the easiest answer is normally the right one and that most people abandon winning ideas earlier than the market does.
Scale up net-new bets only when capacity makes the trade-off cheap.
caveats: The source explicitly says there is no one-size-fits-all answer; these are common-sense defaults, not universal rules.
Bottleneck numbers (10 vs 50 ads/week) are illustrative examples, not benchmarks.

cards.title: Follow a Simple Production Workflow From Idea to Editor
cards.summary: Once the idea is chosen, write hooks first, use AI drafting with light manual edits on mechanism and copy blocks, then hand off to an editor with a winning reference.
cards.use_when: Running the day-to-day production process for paid social assets without overcomplicating the handoff.
steps: Pick the idea from your prioritized test list.
Write one or more hooks for that idea before anything else.
Draft the rest of the ad with AI, doing light manual editing on the major points — especially the mechanism and copy blocks.
The source's view: if the hook is right and the AI writing process is good, the rest of the ad often writes itself.
Produce static images separately, then send video work to an editor paired with a winning reference ad.
Verify the current capabilities of whatever AI production tool you use, since interfaces change.
caveats: Source describes tooling from a specific platform it promotes; the workflow principle transfers, the tooling claims are not independently verified.
AI drafts still need human review for claims, compliance and brand voice.

cards.title: Run a Weekly Refinement Loop and Accept Most Ads Fail
cards.summary: Review your account, competitor accounts and the market multiple times per week, letting data sharpen your decisions while expecting most ads to underperform.
cards.use_when: Setting the operating rhythm for a store's paid social creative program so decisions get updated instead of set once.
steps: Schedule account and competitor reviews at least a few times per week, not just at monthly reporting.
At each review, examine which new ads are winning or losing and why, using the ad DNA and CAST vocabulary.
Update your priorities and focus based on both the data and your developing judgment.
Expect most ads to fail and treat that as normal, not a signal to stop; the job is to keep finding the few that work.
Protect morale and pace by keeping the process mechanical and letting it stay enjoyable, since the source argues enjoyment produces better outcomes.
caveats: The source does not give a specific win-rate percentage, only that most ads fail; don't invent a benchmark.
The link between enjoying the work and outcome quality is the presenter's opinion, not a tested finding.

cards.title: Develop Taste by Deliberately Practicing Ad Diagnosis
cards.summary: Treat intuition as a trainable, mechanical output of repeatedly analyzing ads and forming hypotheses, not a mystical gift.
cards.use_when: Leveling up your own or a team member's creative judgment so faster, better test-prioritization decisions get made for the store.
steps: Practice decomposing many ads — winners and losers — into the DNA and CAST elements on a regular basis.
After each observation, write a hypothesis about why the ad performs as it does.
Watch for subtle, hard-to-articulate patterns across many ads; the source compares this to expert intuition documented in examples like chicken sexers in the book Blink.
Use those accumulated instincts specifically at the prioritization stage, where the source says taste matters most.
Keep the practice mechanical and explicit rather than waiting for intuition to arrive on its own.
caveats: Intuition can encode bias from limited exposure; keep testing hypotheses rather than trusting taste blindly.
The chicken-sexer and Blink references are analogies, not evidence about advertising outcomes.

cards.title: Reduce Video Ads to Element Rotation for Efficient Iteration
cards.summary: Hold the winning element constant and deliberately vary exactly one other element per test to learn what actually drives performance.
cards.use_when: Scaling a proven video ad into a batch of variants for a store without wasting editor time on unfocused changes.
steps: Start from a confirmed winner and list its CAST plus messaging elements.
Form a hypothesis about the active ingredient — the concept, the actor, or their combination.
If the actor is the driver, produce more ads with a comparable actor and swap angle, mechanism, hook and format.
If the concept is the driver, keep the concept and change actor, style, terrain or setup.
If concept and actor both matter in combination, hold both and vary angle, mechanism, hook, or the conceit (e.g. podcast, on-stage talk, street interview, slice-of-life film).
Label each variant by the single changed element so results attribute cleanly.
caveats: Changing only one element per test is cleaner for attribution but slower; the source permits bolder multi-element bets as situational alternatives.
Platform algorithms may serve variants against each other unpredictably; interpret results with caution.

cards.title: Diagnose an Ad by Mapping It to Segment, Concept, Angle and Mechanism
cards.summary: Use a worked breakdown of a real ad to check whether your own creative clearly names who it targets and what idea and mechanism it carries.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a draft ad or existing top performer for a store to see if the underlying idea is strong enough before scaling spend.
steps: Write one line each for: segment (who), concept (core idea), angle (how it's presented), mechanism (problem cause plus solution cause), copy blocks present, hook, and format.

Compare against the source's diabetic men with ED example: segment = diabetic men with ED; concept = high blood sugar scars arteries, harming erections; angle = personified object; mechanism = five science-backed ingredients; all copy blocks present but proof weak; format = personified body part.
Check coherence: does the mechanism connect the problem cause to the solution cause in a simple, intuitive, new way?
Check completeness: which copy blocks are missing or weak and is the hook isolated, committed, deep-fried and loaded with open loops?
Use the diagnosis to fix the weakest layer first rather than reshooting the whole ad.
caveats: These are example ads from the presenter's accounts; replicating a mechanism does not promise the same result in another market.
Health-related mechanisms require substantiation and compliant claims.
